title: Farming under pressure: fisheries, disease control, SFI and land use
label: 27 October 2026 · The future of farming
summary: Ministers and officials from DEFRA told MPs they are trying to support fishing communities, tackle animal disease, speed up water resilience and fix problems with environmental payments. The session exposed clear tensions: fish stock negotiations and Norway access, high costs for farmers from bluetongue and TB testing, a controversial pig-stunning consultation, and a major failure in the Sustainable Farming Incentive window that left many farmers without support. DEFRA accepts lessons must be learned and promises policy work, more engagement and further detail in coming weeks.

glossary.definition: Total allowable catch: the amount of a fish species that countries agree may be caught in a year.
International Council for the Exploration of the Sea: provides scientific advice on marine stocks.
Marine Management Organisation: UK regulator for marine activities, including fisheries.
Sustainable Farming Incentive: a DEFRA payment scheme that pays farmers for specific environmental actions.
Environmental Land Management schemes: DEFRA’s suite of public-money-for-public-goods farming schemes including SFI, Higher Tier and Landscape Recovery.
Animal and Plant Health Agency: government agency that tests and responds to animal disease outbreaks.
The Pirbright Institute: research centre that works on infectious animal diseases and testing.
Sanitary and Phytosanitary agreement: trade rules on animal and plant health measures affecting imports and exports.
Rural Payments Agency: body that administers payments to farmers on behalf of DEFRA.
Site of Special Scientific Interest: protected areas designated for conservation of wildlife or geology.
An ELM scheme that funds long-term, large-scale environmental projects involving multiple landowners.
A higher-tier ELM payment that supports targeted on-farm environmental actions.

chapters.title: Fisheries: engagement, negotiations and Norway access
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA says negotiations will follow science; fishing communities want a clear strategy and fairer access deals with Norway.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You were reappointed as a Minister — does being a Parliamentary Under-Secretary change how you can do the job?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: No — the grades differ but my role is the same: listen to the sector, act on evidence and support resilience across farming and fisheries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Our report suggested regional management groups and a sea-use framework — you rejected those. Why?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We already engage through regional fisheries groups and the MMO. I want engagement to be meaningful and drive a thriving, sustainable industry.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will you produce a fisheries strategy within 12 months?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I recognise we lack a clear fisheries strategy; I'll work with officials and the sector to set a long-term vision, and I'm meeting the APPG soon.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who leads the year-end quota negotiations?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: DEFRA officials lead them; Gareth sets out the science-led parameters I approve and I will engage where needed.

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: Our starting point is ICES science. It set up a tiger team on northern shelf cod; advisers sent us a letter thanking UK scientists for their input.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: ICES advised a zero TAC for northern shelf cod. Is treating three sub-stocks as one sensible?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: ICES manages those sub-stocks as a single northern-shelf stock for TAC setting. Scientists are still working on sub-stock uncertainty and recovery potential.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Norway caught 22,581 tonnes of whitefish in UK waters last year; the UK took 9,496 tonnes in Norwegian waters — how did that imbalance happen?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I raised the issue in Norway and recognise the concerns. Access is reciprocal under current arrangements and is under review in these negotiations.

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: There is an overall balance in access but some parts of the UK fleet — Shetland, for example — feel disadvantaged. We’re engaging with the sector to secure the best UK position.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Saithe: large foreign trips can take big shares of quota and catch immature fish. Does last year's deal help or hinder the stock?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: We factor catch composition and stock condition into TACs. Bycatch and spatial measures are part of the conversation—these are live, complicated issues.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fuel costs are forcing boats to stay ashore. Will you match EU state aids to help our fleet?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We’re monitoring fuel pressures and have existing tax-based fuel support. Calls exist to reallocate funds like the coastal growth fund; we’re looking at options.

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: The sector asked if money could be reallocated. Officials are working through whether that is possible; any change is a ministerial decision.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will an SPS agreement with the EU affect the UK’s sovereign fisheries management?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: We are not worried about losing sovereign fishing policy since we left the CFP; we will protect UK interests.

chapters.title: Animal disease: bluetongue, TB and testing
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA expanded testing and supported vaccine supply for bluetongue, rejects subsidising vaccines, will publish next TB delivery steps before Christmas.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Bluetongue this year has been devastating—high disposal costs and fertility losses. What support will you give affected farmers?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I’ve visited affected farms. DEFRA helped secure vaccine supply, eased some admin, funded veterinary support, expanded testing and improved case maps; we’re doing lessons learned work.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Some EU countries subsidise vaccination. Will you?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We’re not moving to mandatory or subsidised vaccination now; vaccination is a farm decision with vets. Costs are typically £2.50–£3 per dose.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Communication delays left farmers feeling they lost the chance to vaccinate early. Who was responsible?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: DEFRA led a partnership response—APHA, Pirbright, NFU—and ran webinars and blogs. There are lessons to learn and we will improve communications.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: On bovine TB: when will you respond to the June control strategy and how will you reduce false reactors on tests?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We’ve adopted the TB control strategy and will publish the next steps before Christmas. We’re developing cattle vaccines, rolling out badger vaccination and expanding interferon-gamma testing.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Work is underway on blood testing and other measures to improve detection and limit unnecessary slaughter; we’ll look at options the Committee raised.

chapters.title: Abattoirs and slaughter welfare: CO2 consultation and capacity
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA has launched a consultation to phase out CO2 stunning for pigs as part of an animal welfare roadmap; industry warns evidence is weak and abattoir capacity is constrained.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: You’ve opened a consultation on replacing CO2 with argon or electric stunning, but trials show welfare problems and practical challenges. Is the evidence strong enough?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: The consultation reflects the animal welfare strategy; we’ve engaged industry and want views. The consultation will gather the evidence to inform Ministers.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: The consultation is to collect industry evidence on methods and impacts. It follows the Animal Welfare Committee’s recommendations and will inform decisions.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Industry says there were no proper trials and abattoirs may need two to three years and major conversions. Meanwhile 15,000 pigs are already backed up on farms—will your planned summit address the immediate welfare risk?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I’ll convene industry, processors and others at a summit to discuss market monitoring, forecasting and how Government can help avoid short-term welfare problems.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: Argon and nitrogen are produced largely abroad; relying on imports could affect food security. Do you accept supply-chain risks?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We’ll look at those logistical concerns as part of the consultation and follow-up with industry.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: Small abattoirs are collapsing; around 2,500 in the 1970s to 200 today. Will you treat abattoirs as critical infrastructure and consider a dedicated fund?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We work with an abattoir group and task forces; we’re exploring regulatory relief and other measures. The closed Smaller Abattoir Fund is under review for alternatives.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We’re also looking at reducing inspection burdens and other proportionate regulatory changes to help smaller abattoirs survive.

chapters.title: Water, reservoirs and drought resilience
chapters.takeaway: Government has funds for on-farm reservoirs but planning and abstraction licences cause delays; cross-government action is underway to speed approvals.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Farmers need fast decisions on abstraction licences now — seed orders are due but licences expire next March. When will the process be easier?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We announced a £15m water-management grant; the detail is coming next month. We’re working across Government, including MHCLG, to speed planning and licensing and set milestones agreed at the partnership board.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We’re taking a system-wide look: planning, Natural England screening, Environment Agency licences and tech solutions like smart abstraction monitoring are all on the table.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: You announced £50m reallocated to SFI for drought resilience; why wasn’t that ring-fenced for reservoirs?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We prioritised getting applications open quickly; ring-fencing would have required system changes that would have slowed delivery. We’ll consider options for next year.

chapters.title: SFI and ELMs: the failed window and the fallout
chapters.takeaway: Window 2 of SFI closed within hours and left many farmers without agreements; DEFRA accepts lessons must be learned and will change first-come, first-served, but funding constraints remain central.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Window 2 opened at 10am and shut within six hours. How many expiring agreements did you expect and what budget did you set?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We had over 20,000 expiring agreements and expected high demand. Window 2 received around 12,200 applications. The scheme’s budget was increased from about £180m to roughly £253m after extra funding.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: The NFU says expiring agreements were worth £520m but the two windows had £310m — where’s the £210m gap?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Those figures assume every expiring agreement would transfer into SFI; some land moves to higher-tier schemes or landscape recovery. Money isn’t ‘missing’ but the funding envelope is finite and allocations were reassessed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You kept first come, first served despite clear signs of oversubscription. Why wasn’t the window paused and redesigned?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: The scheme design and timetable were set before my appointment. I accept lessons must be learned. I’ve committed to end first-come, first-served and to co-design changes with the sector.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Farmers were left without certainty; many say DEFRA set them up to fail. How will you prevent a repeat?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We’ll scrap first-come, first-served, review actions, payment rates and caps, and work with stakeholders on a fairer allocation system for next year.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: RPA is checking exceptions reported after closure. How many cases and will those applicants get agreements?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: There are two groups—those who asked for digital help and those who reported system issues. RPA is checking case by case; our preliminary estimate of affected payments is under £5m but the figure will be clarified.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: SFI funds public goods, not basic income. But many farms may now have no public support. How will you support farms left outside the schemes?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: SFI never aimed to be universal income support. We are trying to spread finite public money where it produces the best environmental outcomes while supporting productivity through other policies.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: Private nature markets are supposed to fill gaps. Farmers say those markets don’t exist for upland or small farms. What are you doing?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We published 'Growing Places' and set up a private-finance working group to identify where markets work, the barriers and conditions for success. It’s early work but a priority.

chapters.title: Uplands, Landscape Recovery and countryside stewardship
chapters.takeaway: Upland communities fear cliff-edge funding and heavy-handed conservation rules; DEFRA pledges local engagement, targeted transitions and legal reviews.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: What will uplands look like in 20 years? Is livestock central or a problem to manage?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I want uplands to be productive and nature-rich. It’s not binary: grazing management must be tailored by place. Dr Hilary Cottam’s community-led work on Dartmoor is a useful model.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: There are 5,400 higher-level stewardship agreements expiring in 2027–28. Will Natural England and RPA have capacity to replace them without cliff edges?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We’re taking a cohort-by-cohort approach: some expiring agreements can move straight into higher tier; others need tailored handling, especially where SSSIs are involved. Natural England is working through cohorts now.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Dartmoor figures show proposed de-stocking levels of around 76% in some places. Is that DEFRA policy or Natural England’s?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Natural England advises on SSSI condition and required actions. We are working with them and local groups to find solutions that reduce overwintering pressure but avoid one-size-fits-all measures.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Common land is still excluded from SFI because of legacy software issues. When will that be fixed?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: RPA is piloting fixes to put higher-tier stewardship on the system and address common-land eligibility. It’s an old technical barrier and we're working to resolve it.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Landscape Recovery has 56 projects in development but only three in implementation. Why so slow?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: The projects are complex, involve many landowners and carry long-term public money. We’re advising on simplifying governance and speeding up transitions where we can.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Landscape Recovery is innovative and therefore implementation is harder than SFI. Ministers have asked for practical advice to open the pipeline without diluting outcomes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We will follow up in writing on many of these issues. Thank you for coming today.
